newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr on a yen high amid rate relief.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr on a yen high amid rate relief.

text.p: The Australian dollar sprang ahead Wednesday, capturing a four-year high on the yen after fears of an imminent rate cut were salved by Reserve Bank silence.
Speculation had been rife the central bank would ease policy this morning following its monthly board meeting on Tuesday, but the normal window for a move came and went with no announcement.

"The AUD's won a reprieve from the negative sentiment that was building about a rate cut," said Steve Shuster, head of forex at Citibank Australia. "It's had a good run on the yen, but an easing is still a risk so I wouldn't get carried away."
By 4.30 pm the dollar had surged to 88.74/84 yen from 87.71/81 late Tuesday, surpassing its July rally peak of 88.50 and breaking into territory not seen since September 1992.

The Japanese enthusiasm spilled over into a broad-based rally taking it to US$0.7935/40 from an early US$0.7905/10 and US$0.7910/15 late here Tuesday. In trade weighted terms it jumped to 58.7 from a previous 58.4 close.

The RBA's inaction came a relief to bulls as a cut in domestic rates would have left the currency's yield premium over the U.S. dollar at unappealingly thin levels, which might well have choked off the Japanese appetite for A$ samurais.
Japanese retail demand for relatively high yielding A$-denominated dual currency samurais bonds has been a major source of support for the currency this year.
Dealers ssupected much of the buying today was linked with fresh samurai issues and even reported rumours a single Japanese securities house bought as much as A$1.0 billion for yen.
They saw scope for the currency to test 89.00 yen and US$0.7950 in the near term, but cautioned that the market still thought an RBA easing likely before year end.
"We continue to expect another official cut in cash rates," said John Kyriakopoulos, senior economist at Macquarie Bank.
Such an easing could be justified by an improvement in inflation and inflation expectations, rather than as a stimulant for economic activity, Macquarie said.
In this regard third quarter inflation data on October 23 and wages figures the day after would be crucial.
"Underlying inflation could rise less than expected, and a moderate rise in wages would pave the way for a rate cut after the RBA's November 5 board meeting," Kyiriakopoulos said.
The money market seemed to agree and kept the 90-day bank bill futures contract steady at 93.40, implying an interest rate of 6.60 percent against the present official 7.00 percent.
The local dollar's yield advantage had also looked a little safer from the perspective of U.S. rate trends after the Federal Reserve declined to tighten policy last week.
That sparked tak the Fed might not have to raise rates at all this year, a premise that seemed to be supported by comments -- strangely enough -- from Australian Treasurer Peter Costello.
Talking to journalists after meeting Fed chairman Alan Greenspan in Washington on Monday, Costello said Greenspan had indicated that he saw no threats to inflation down the track.
"So he indicated to me that there was no reason to expect a change on current scene as he sees it," Costello said.
Costello later played down the remarks, but by then the U.S. bond market had rallied in anticipation of a steady Fed policy.
Elsewhere, there was talk of potential A$ demand linked to a A$2.0 billion agreed bid for Australian transport group TNT by Dutch postal and telecommunications group KPN.
Dealers, however, suspected much of the currency exposure had been covered in the last week or two, largely in the options market, and the net effect would be slight.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
